record.paper_title: Open Problems in the Topology of Manifolds
record.original_question: For Cat equal to Top, PL, or Diff, call a Cat-manifold irreducible when every connected-sum decomposition of it has at least one summand that is a homotopy sphere. In dimension 3, the Kneser-Milnor theorem says that every compact Cat 3-manifold decomposes as a connected sum of irreducible 3-manifolds and that the decomposition is unique up to permutation of summands. To what extent do the existence and uniqueness parts of this connected-sum decomposition theorem hold for compact Cat-manifolds in dimensions at least 4, allowing the formulation to be taken up to homotopy spheres?

evidence.quote: Let Cat be one of the categories Top, PL or Diff. A Cat-manifold M is called irreducible if, whenever we can write M as a connected sum of Cat-manifolds at least one of the summands is a homotopy sphere.

The Kneser-Milnor theorem says that every compact Cat 3-manifold admits a connected sum decomposition into irreducible 3-manifolds, and this connected sum decomposition is unique up to permutation of the summands. Stefan Friedl asked to what degree this statement holds in higher dimensions.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let Cat be one of the categories Top (topological), PL (piecewise-linear), or Diff (smooth). A compact connected Cat-manifold M is said to be irreducible if, whenever M is expressed as a connected sum M ≅ N_1 # N_2 of compact Cat-manifolds, at least one of N_1, N_2 is a homotopy sphere. The Kneser–Milnor theorem asserts that, in dimension 3, every compact Cat 3-manifold decomposes as a connected sum of finitely many irreducible Cat 3-manifolds, and that the decomposition is unique up to permutation of the summands.

Investigate to what extent the analogous statement holds in each dimension n ≥ 4 and for each Cat ∈ {Top, PL, Diff}, where the decomposition is taken up to homotopy spheres (i.e., one identifies any two decompositions that differ by inserting or removing homotopy-sphere summands and by permuting summands). Specifically, determine:

(a) (Existence) Does every compact connected Cat n-manifold admit a connected-sum decomposition into finitely many irreducible Cat-manifolds?

(b) (Uniqueness) Is any such decomposition unique up to permutation of summands and modification by homotopy-sphere summands?

Provide either proofs of existence and uniqueness in each case, or explicit counterexamples that demonstrate their failure, as functions of the dimension n and the category Cat.
artifact.status_search_result: The question has been partially resolved. Existence of connected-sum decompositions into irreducible manifolds (up to homotopy spheres) has been established in many high-dimensional cases. Uniqueness, however, is known to fail in general: Cappell exhibited counterexamples to the Kneser conjecture in higher dimensions, and Kreck–Lück–Teichner showed failure of uniqueness in dimension 4. Subsequent work (e.g., Bokor–Crowley–Friedl–Hebestreit–Kasprowski–Land–Nicholson) gives unique factorization theorems in particular dimensions and categories (e.g., for simply connected manifolds in even dimensions ≥ 4) while non-uniqueness persists in other settings. A complete characterization across all (n, Cat) remains incomplete.

status_evidence.title: Connected sum decompositions of high-dimensional manifolds
status_evidence.snippet: Survey on the existence and uniqueness of connected sum decompositions in high dimensions, addressing Friedl's question.
status_evidence.claim: The problem has been actively studied and is partially resolved; uniqueness fails in general but holds in specific dimensions/categories.

status_evidence.title: Prime decomposition theorem in high dimensions - Manifold Atlas
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses dimension- and category-dependent unique factorisation results and failures for connected sums in dimensions ≥ 4.
status_evidence.claim: Uniqueness holds in some cases and fails in others depending on dimension and category.
